title: GPU-accelerated semidefinite programming for causal games
abstract: The process matrix formalism describes quantum correlations in scenarios without a fixed causal order between local laboratories. Operational signatures of such correlations can be investigated through causal games. A paradigmatic example is the Guess-Your-Neighbour's-Input game, in which two parties attempt to guess each other's inputs. Correlations compatible with any definite, or probabilistically mixed, causal order cannot achieve a winning probability exceeding $1/2$. The best process-matrix strategy currently known attains a value of approximately $0.6218$ using local dimension $d=5$, while the strongest known dimension-independent upper bound is $0.7592$. In this work, we investigate whether increasing the local dimension beyond $d = 5$ can narrow this gap. To this end, we employ a see-saw optimization scheme in which each step is formulated as a semidefinite program. For scalability, we develop a custom implementation of the SCS solver in which the dominant computational cost, the projection onto the positive-semidefinite cone, is offloaded to a GPU, yielding a six-fold speedup. Using this implementation, we explore local dimensions up to $d = 8$, and we do not find significant improvements over the value at $d=5$. Our results suggest that either qualitatively different strategies are required to approach the known upper bound, or that the bound itself is not tight.
summary: This work uses GPU-accelerated Semidefinite Programming to study quantum correlations violating definite causal order via the GYNI game. The authors test if increasing local dimension improves the achievable bound but find diminishing returns. This suggests that improving the theoretical upper bound or finding fundamentally different strategies is necessary.
main_problem: The research investigates whether increasing the local dimension ($d$) can narrow the gap between the best known process-matrix strategy value ($\approx 0.6218$) and the strongest upper bound for correlations violating definite causal order in the Guess-Your-Neighbour's-Input (GYNI) game.
main_result: The study found no significant improvement in the winning probability when increasing the local dimension up to $d=8$, suggesting that either qualitatively different strategies are needed or the known upper bound is not tight.
method: Optimization relies on formulating the problem as a sequence of Semidefinite Programs (SDPs) solved using a see-saw optimization scheme, significantly accelerated by offloading the projection onto the positive-semidefinite cone to a GPU.
model_or_system: The study analyzes quantum correlations described by the process matrix formalism, which models scenarios lacking a fixed causal order between local laboratories. The paradigmatic example is the bipartite GYNI game used to test for violations of definite causal orders.
key_observables: Winning probability ($\omega_{GYNI}$) in the GYNI game; violation of causal inequalities.
important_parameters: Local dimension ($d$); best known strategy value ($\approx 0.6218$); upper bound ($\approx 0.7592$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the optimal correlations can be captured within the process matrix formalism and that SDP solvers provide sufficient accuracy.
figures_summary: Table I summarizes $\omega_{GYNI}$ as a function of $d$, showing slow growth; Table IV compares computational time for solving representative SDPs across increasing dimensions, highlighting GPU speedups.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework using process matrices and causal games, details the optimization via see-saw SDPs, implements this efficiently on GPUs, and concludes by analyzing the scaling of the achievable bound with local dimension $d$.
why_interesting: It provides advanced computational techniques (GPU-accelerated SDP solving) to probe fundamental questions about causality in quantum mechanics, which is highly relevant for understanding resource theories beyond standard entanglement.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic representation of the bipartite scenario within the process matrix formalism. Given local instruments Ca|x and Cb|y, the process matrix W assigns joint probabilities p(ab|xy) = tr[W(Ca|x⊗Cb|y)] for all settings x, y and outcomes a, b.

FIG. 2. Residual evolution for a representative process-matrix SDP with local dimension d = 4. The reference implemen- tation is SCS 3.2.11 with all default settings, except that data normalization is disabled in both solvers. The residual histories agree almost exactly on an iteration-by-iteration ba- sis, confirming that the implementations produce the same ADMM iterates. The discrepancy in the final iteration number is due solely to the termination-check frequency: SCS eval- uates convergence every 25 iterations and therefore reports residuals up to iteration 275, whereas our implementation checks convergence every iteration and terminates at iteration 264.
